column4: The command to spend from what God has made people successors over treats present possession as a temporary stewardship, directly joining spending to the section's claim about ultimate inheritance.
Those dividing an estate must imagine leaving their own weak offspring behind and speak rightly, bringing the vulnerable child's future into the inheritance scene.
The prohibition on inheriting women by compulsion exposes another abuse hidden under inheritance language: treating a vulnerable person herself as property to be seized.
The verse appoints heirs for what parents and relatives leave and commands that contracted associates be given their share, another explicit barrier against swallowing the estate whole.
When death approaches one who leaves wealth, a fair bequest for parents and near relatives is prescribed, directing the departing owner's store toward named claimants.
Concerning orphans, reform is best; if their property is mixed with the guardian's, they remain brothers, and God knows the corrupter from the reformer.
Do not approach orphan property except in the best manner until maturity, a direct boundary around the vulnerable heir's share.
After the commands for honest measure, the remainder left by God is declared better than wrongful gain, reversing the fear that fairness empties one's vessel.
The short-measurers are asked whether they expect to be resurrected, making final accountability the reason a commercial measure cannot be manipulated.
The resurrection is for a tremendous day, locating the apparently small theft from another's measure inside judgment.
People will stand before the Lord of the worlds, the endpoint at which every underfilled share is answered.
God gives life and death and declares that He is the inheritor, a compact statement of the section's claim that all possession finally returns to the One who remains.
Some covenant that if God gives them from His bounty they will give charity and become righteous, making promised sharing depend on received provision.
When God gives them from His bounty they become stingy and turn away, staging the full vessel's closure at the moment it is filled.
Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the day they meet God, giving retained bounty an inward consequence.
Owners must give contracted dependents from the wealth God gave them, so divine gift creates a claim for release and liberation rather than permanent control.
Asked what to spend, the answer is the surplus beyond need, identifying what should leave a vessel rather than accumulate in it.
A good loan to God is multiplied many times, while God constricts and expands; true increase comes through giving within His measure.
Open charity is good, but hidden charity given to the poor is better, keeping the needy person's receipt central while removing the giver's display.
God destroys usurious increase and causes charities to grow, reversing the accumulator's account of what diminishes and what multiplies.
The one who lends God a good loan has it multiplied and receives a generous reward, making released wealth the source of lasting increase.
Charitable men and women who lend God well have their gift multiplied, another explicit reversal of increase through retention.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, so the portion leaving one's hand is not the portion finally lost.
The question asks whether the extension of wealth and sons is being mistaken for God hastening good things to its recipients.
The answer is that they do not perceive, directly correcting the assumption that abundant provision itself certifies honor.
The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, the precise false reading answered by divine expansion and restriction in 34:36.
Neither wealth nor children bring anyone near to God; faithful good action instead receives multiplied reward and secure dwellings.
The Prophet is told not to admire their wealth and children, for God wills to punish them through those very possessions in worldly life.
The warning not to admire wealth and children is repeated, again turning apparent abundance into an instrument of punishment rather than honor.
After hardship, a person calls on God, then attributes the granted favor to personal knowledge; the verse calls it a trial, matching the section's correction of self-credit for provision.
After adversity, a recipient of mercy says it is his and doubts the Hour, exposing how a granted share becomes a claim of permanent ownership.
The question who denies the Judgment identifies the stance embodied by repelling the orphan and refusing to urge needy-food in the next two ayat.
The closing charge that they withhold small acts of aid extends the closed table from food to ordinary useful things neighbors need.
The left-hand recipient says his authority has perished after saying wealth did not avail, so both stored property and the power built around it collapse.
The people of the right ask the offenders what brought them into Saqar, introducing the confession that includes failure to feed the needy.
The offenders first confess that they were not among those who prayed, preserving the co-cause stated beside refusal to feed in 74:44.
The feeders say they feed only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, showing how the beloved food is released without creating a new claim over its recipients.
The astray are told they will eat from the tree of Zaqqum, turning voracious worldly eating into a punitive meal.
They will fill their bellies from Zaqqum, a bodily container filled with the opposite of sustaining provision.
They then drink scalding water over the hellish food, continuing the reversed table.
Their drinking is like desperately thirsty camels, so even a filled belly produces no sufficiency.
The tree of Zaqqum is introduced as the food awaiting the grave sinner, reversing food from support into punishment.
طَعَامُ ٱلْأَثِيمِ explicitly names Zaqqum as the sinner's food.
The food is like molten metal boiling in bellies, joining eating to an internal fire.
Its boiling is compared with boiling scalding water, completing the transformation of the meal into flame-like torment.
The humbled have no food except a bitter thorn, a punitive counterpart to the sustaining food withheld from the needy.
That food neither nourishes nor removes hunger, exactly negating the section's idea that provision enables a weak person to remain.
Disbelievers eat as cattle eat and the Fire is their lodging, placing unreflective consumption on a direct path to Hell.
Those who conceal revelation for a small price eat only fire into their bellies, a close parallel to orphan-property becoming fire in 4:10.
The demanded sign is an offering consumed by fire, giving the section's cited dictionary sense of fire 'eating' something a direct Quranic scene.
A garden heavy with fruit is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its aged owner has weak offspring, joining abundant food, vulnerable dependents, and consuming fire in one loss.
God splits the grain and date-stone and brings life from death, supplying a direct Quranic use of the grain-sense of h-b-b developed by the section.
Rain produces vegetation and clustered grain, locating the jar's imagined grain within a visible chain of divine provision.
The earth holds grain with husks among its provisions, another direct occurrence of the h-b-b grain sense.
Rain is sent so that grain and vegetation may be brought forth, joining the secondary grain sense to divine supply.
Water descends بِقَدَرٍۢ and is lodged in the earth, uniting measure, gathered water, storage, and God's ability to remove it.
God sends water from heaven بِقَدَرٍۢ and revives dead land, making measured release rather than limitless filling the source of life.
إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَٰهُ بِقَدَرٍۢ gives the section's universal claim that every thing has a measure its concise Quranic formulation.
God creates every thing and determines it with exact determination, grounding all shares and limits in creation itself.
The she-camel has a drinking share and the people a drinking share on an appointed day, a concrete division of one water source into measured turns.
Twelve springs emerge, each group knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink from God's provision without corruption.
The twelve tribes each know their spring while manna and quails are provided, a scene where water and food are apportioned to a whole community.
The divorced woman receives a fair provision according to the wealthy or constrained giver's capacity, applying measure to a vulnerable person's material due.
Divorced women are assigned a fair provision as a duty on the mindful, another named share that must leave an owner's wealth.
The righteous servants inherit the earth, relocating inheritance from predatory seizure to the final outcome promised by God.
The faithful qualities make their bearers the heirs, introducing an inheritance defined by character rather than accumulation.
Those heirs inherit Firdaus and remain there, setting lasting inheritance against the perishable legacy people consume unjustly.
Paradise is the garden God gives as inheritance to mindful servants, an inheritance received from divine promise rather than taken from the weak.
The people of Paradise praise God for letting them inherit the land and settle wherever they wish, a lasting dwelling granted after worldly stores end.
Paradise is declared the inheritance given because of deeds, reversing inheritance from an object of appetite into a moral outcome.
Men and women each have a share of what they earn, and envy is redirected into asking God from His bounty, preserving distinct portions under divine giving.
Blood relatives are declared closer to one another in God's Book, establishing the kinship order within which inherited property is apportioned.
Blood relatives are closer to one another in God's decree than other affiliations, another boundary preserving the proper recipients of a legacy.
The mindful spend from what God has provided them, turning rizq into circulation rather than treating it as a sealed personal stock.
True believers spend from divine provision, making release of the allotted share part of their response to God.
Those who spend from provision secretly and openly are placed among people seeking God's face, the opposite stance from hoarding for permanence.
Believers must spend from provision secretly and openly before a day without trade or friendship, giving the allotted share a finite time for use.
Those given double reward spend from what God provided them, linking received gift to outgoing support.
Those who leave their beds in fear and hope also spend from divine provision, pairing dependence on God with opening the vessel.
Those who answer their Lord conduct affairs by mutual consultation and spend from provision, a positive communal counterpart to failing to urge one another toward feeding.
If humans possessed the treasures of God's mercy, they would still withhold for fear of spending; the verse diagnoses the impulse behind the sealed full vessel.
Humanity is described as anxiously grasping, introducing the response to good and harm that explains the gatherer and stower later in the passage.
When harm touches the anxious person, he becomes impatient, one side of the insecurity that accumulation tries to master.
When good touches him, he becomes withholding, the exact inward motion that closes provision against other claimants.
Do not keep the hand chained to the neck or extend it without limit; the commanded middle regulates both hoarding and ruinous emptying.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily but hold a just balance between them, a moral measure for the vessel.
Hypocrites urge one another toward wrong, forbid right, and close their hands, a communal inverse of reciprocal urging toward the needy person's food.
Were God to press people for all their wealth, they would become stingy and their resentments would emerge; the verse exposes the resistance named in 47:38.
People are told to seek provision from God, worship Him, and give thanks, locating the source of every share before its human holder.
God seeks no provision from people and does not ask them to feed Him, reversing any idea that the Provider depends on the stocked vessel.
God alone is the Provider and possessor of firm power, grounding all human provision and feeding in His sufficiency.
إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَرِزْقُنَا مَا لَهُۥ مِن نَّفَادٍۢ describes divine provision as inexhaustible, unlike the finite stores people guard.
Do not stretch the eyes toward worldly splendor used as a test; the Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
Mary receives provision in the sanctuary and identifies God as its source, who provides without account, a scene of sustenance arriving beyond ordinary control.
The condemned assignment is called قِسْمَةٌۭ ضِيزَىٰ, an unjust division, supplying a direct Quranic judgment on corrupted apportionment.
Earlier peoples had greater wealth and children and enjoyed their allotted share; the addressees likewise enjoy their share and plunge as they did, joining abundance, portion, and moral loss.
The condemned man is reminded that God gave him extensive wealth, locating the filled store as a gift rather than self-made possession.
ثُمَّ يَطْمَعُ أَنْ أَزِيدَ shows the recipient of extensive wealth still craving that God add more, the full vessel's unsatisfied appetite.
The answer كَلَّآ sets a firm refusal against his demand for still more.
Noah describes people following leaders whose wealth and children increase them only in loss, reversing abundance from success into ruin.
The verse gathers loved relatives, acquired wealth, feared commercial decline, and pleasing dwellings, then tests whether these are loved more than God and His cause.
Solomon says he loved fine possessions over remembrance until they were hidden, a non-monetary instance of love filling attention and displacing what should govern it.
The boat belongs to needy people who work at sea and faces confiscation by a king, showing that a miskin can possess productive property yet remain weak before power.
Poor emigrants driven from homes and property seek God's bounty, making material deprivation a loss of dwelling and livelihood rather than mere lack of coins.
God makes houses a place of rest and provides portable dwellings, developing the s-k-n sense through the material means that let people remain somewhere.
A good dwelling with two gardens is called a sign, and its people are told to eat from their Lord's provision and thank Him.
When warnings are forgotten, the doors of every thing are opened; at the moment of exultant fullness the recipients are seized and left despairing.
Gardens and springs are the first possessions Pharaoh's people leave behind before another people inherit them in 44:28.
Crops and noble dwellings add food and settled property to the estate that passes from one people to another.
The comforts in which they delighted complete the inventory of a full life that does not remain with its holders.
Pharaoh's people are removed from gardens and springs, beginning the transfer named as Israel's inheritance in 26:59.
Treasures and an honorable station are added to what the departing people leave for others.
The poorer companion says the garden owner should have acknowledged God's will and power on entering, correcting the claim of self-secured abundance.
After the garden's collapse, true protection belongs to God and His reward and outcome are best, replacing the failed protection of wealth and followers.
On seeing the ruined garden, the owners first think they have lost their way, showing how completely expected abundance has vanished.
The owners glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, the first truthful response after trying to exclude the needy.
They turn on one another in blame, exposing the failed communal counsel behind their shared plan to withhold the crop.
